newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-Telecom commits to earnings growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Telecom commits to earnings growth.

text.p: Telecom Corp of New Zealand on Tuesday pledged to revitalise flagging earnings growth and move aggressively into the new millennium with the rapidly evolving telecommunications industry.

Reporting an 8.0 percent decline in third quarter net earnings to NZ$167.2 million, its first profit fall in four years, Telecom chief Executive Roderick Deane said cost reduction was a major issue for the company.
"That's going to be the name of the game for us, given the way competition is going," Deane said.

Telecom's profit for the nine months to December 31 was $528.1 million, up 1.5 percent. While volumes growth remained strong, competition had seen prices fall, and operating expenses were up 10.7 percent in the nine-month period.
To address it flagging earnings growth, Telecom plans a new series of cost reduction initiatives in 1997/98 and has asked shareholders Ameritech and Bell Atlantic to supply "some expertise".

Deane said Telecom was also actively moving to divest itself of loss-making Australian subsidiary Pacific Star, which depressed the third quarter result by $17 million and the nine-month profit by $39.8 million.
Start-up costs associated with Telecom's Internet service provider Xtra and its First Media cable television network of entertainment and information services had also tugged on earnings.

"I think looking ahead to the future, as we get the Pac Star problems resolved and as we get Xtra and First Media into more strongly operational mode, the major challenge will be productivity improvements and cost control," Deane said.

"So long as we can get our costs down fast enough relative to the price declines and keep growing those business volumes, which we're determined to do, then we will see a resumption of earnings growth as the year progresses."

Deane said margins would continue to decline in the rapidly evolving and increasingly competitive telecommunications industry, and the trick was how to manage those declines in order to continue to grow earnings.
He said Telecom saw mobility and personalisation of telecommunications services as the big trend for the future.

Telecom was developing plans for the commercial launch of a new personal communications service (PCS) which it had been trialing since 1995. PSC combined features from the cellular and fixed-line networks to provide the customer with mobility of communications and other personalised services.
"We really see that the linkage between fixed-wire services and mobile services will be a big driver for our future as well as for the future of the industry," Deane said.

"People will increasingly want services to be personalised to their own needs to be able to adapt to their own particular requirements and be able to carry their phone and their single number with them wherever they wish to."
Telecom would also provide greater band width, partly though its planned cable rollout and partly though other technologies.

"We see that the demand for band width will be very strong over the future years and we're determined to meet that demand from customers, including all of the interactive type services that people will be anxious to have and which we're now seeing coming through in the Internet," Deane said.

Telecom was already trialing telephone calls through the Internet and Deane said a commercial service was expected to be launched later this year. Shopping via the Internet was another "exciting development".

Deane said it was possible that capital expediture would exceed the $700 million already flagged for the 1996/97 financial year, and also noted that the cost of adjusting Telecom's computer systems to accomodate the year 2000 would be "substantial".
